units.text: RELAY: safety and efficacy of ramucirumab plus erlotinib in elderly Japanese patients with metastatic EGFR-mutated NSCLC
Introduction

Lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer, accounting for 12.4% of all cancers worldwide [1].The majority (85%) of lung cancers are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [2].Most lung cancers are diagnosed later in life, with the median age in individual countries ranging from 60 to 74 years [3], and 50% of patients with NSCLC worldwide are aged ≥ 70 years [4].Owing to its aging population, Japan has the highest median age of lung cancer diagnosis at 74 years [3].Despite this, clinical trial data on the safety and efficacy of lung cancer treatments in elderly patients are limited [5].

Mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene are the most common oncogenic drivers of NSCLC in Asian populations [6].The two most common EGFR mutations are a deletion in exon 19 (ex19del) and an amino acid substitution in exon 21 (L858R); although the ex19del mutation is more common than L858R in European and North American populations, the two mutations occur at approximately the same frequency in Japanese patients [7].For patients with EGFR-mutated advanced or metastatic NSCLC, the first-line standard of care is an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) [8][9][10].Although EGFR-TKIs are effective, the use of EGFR-TKI monotherapy is limited by the acquisition of resistance mutations, and tumors eventually progress [11].Thus, alternative treatment strategies, including combination therapies, are increasingly being developed and used clinically, including as first-line therapy [8].Recent trials have demonstrated that combining a third-generation EGFR-TKI with other therapies (e.g., chemotherapy in the FLAURA2 trial [12]; amivantamab, a bispecific antibody against EGFR and the MET receptor in the MARIPOSA trial [13]) results in superior efficacy compared with EGFR-TKI monotherapy.However, the benefits and risks of these combination therapies in elderly patients have not yet been reported.

RELAY was a global, phase III, randomized, placebocontrolled trial that demonstrated the efficacy of ramucirumab (RAM), an inhibitor of angiogenesis, in combination with the EGFR-TKI erlotinib (ERL), in patients with EGFR-mutated advanced or metastatic NSCLC [14,15].

Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 19.4 months in the RAM+ERL arm and 12.4 months in the placebo (PL)+ERL arm (stratified hazard ratio [HR]: 0.59, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.46-0.76) in the global intent-to-treat (ITT) population [15].In the final overall survival (OS) analysis, median OS was 51.1 months with RAM+ERL and 46.0 months with PL+ERL (HR: 0.98 [95% CI: 0.78-1.24])[14].Similar PFS and OS results were observed in the Japanese subset of RELAY [16,17], with a more pronounced OS effect in patients with the L858R mutation than in those with the ex19del mutation [17].Observational studies of RAM+ERL in Japanese patients currently underway (e.g., REAL-SPEED [18]) will provide additional insights into the benefits of this combination therapy in the Japanese population.In RELAY, approximately 13% of the global ITT population and 14% of the Japanese ITT population were aged ≥ 75 years.In this age group, median OS in Japanese patients was 44.2 months with RAM+ERL versus 36.3 months with PL+ERL (HR: 0.91 [95% CI: 0.40-2.09]),with a survival benefit of 8.0 months, which is similar to that seen in patients aged < 75 years (survival benefit of 8.1 months) [17].

Clinical data on risk/benefit in elderly patients with NSCLC are needed to provide clinicians with evidence for selecting appropriate treatment strategies [19][20][21].Japan's lung cancer treatment guidelines state that for patients with driver gene mutations, targeted therapy is generally less toxic than cytotoxic anticancer drugs and is expected to be relatively safe for elderly people, defined as aged ≥ 75 years [5].As such, treatment strategies involving targeted therapies that delay subsequent chemotherapy for as long as possible are especially important in elderly patients.However, there are no previous studies that have specifically evaluated the safety and efficacy of combination therapy in elderly Japanese patients (≥ 75 years) with EGFR-mutated NSCLC.This represents a significant evidence gap.Recent global trials evaluating EGFR-TKI-based combination therapies, such as FLAURA2 [12] and MARIPOSA [13], included only limited numbers of Japanese patients overall (FLAURA2: 94 patients [16.9%] [22]; MARIPOSA: 78 patients [7.3%] [23]), as well as low numbers of elderly patients.As such, these studies do not provide sufficient data to inform treatment decisions in the elderly Japanese population.

Here, we present safety and efficacy profiles, including response rates, study drug exposures, dose adjustments, and poststudy treatment discontinuation therapies, in Japanese RELAY patients aged ≥ 75 years treated with RAM+ERL.
Materials and methods
Study design and study population
The RELAY study design (www.clinicaltrials.gov:NCT02411448; registered 3 April 2015) has been described
Article highlights

• This is the first analysis to evaluate the risks and benefits of an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitorbased combination therapy in elderly Japanese patients with EGFRmutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Outcomes

The primary endpoint of PFS and the secondary endpoint of OS have been reported previously for the global [14,15] and Japanese ITT [16,17] populations.The results of post hoc analyses of PFS [16] and OS [17] in Japanese elderly (aged ≥ 75 years) patients have also been reported.Secondary efficacy endpoints reported herein for Japanese elderly patients in the RAM+ERL and PL+ERL arms include best overall response, objective response rate (complete response and partial response), and disease control rate (complete response, partial response, and stable disease).Overall response was based on tumor assessments (computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) conducted every 6 weeks for the first 72 weeks, then every 12 weeks until progression or study discontinuation, and again at 30 days' follow-up.Responses were also analyzed by treatment arm and EGFR mutation.

For safety, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were designated using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities Version 26.0 and graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v4.0.Interstitial lung disease (ILD) and pneumonitis were also recorded as TEAEs of interest.

Study drug exposure and relative dose intensity for RAM/PL and for ERL are reported, and subsequent therapies post study drug discontinuation are summarized.Time to chemotherapy or death is also reported.Data cutoff for all results was 20 October 2023 (final OS analysis).
Statistical analysis

All analyses were post hoc, and the results are presented descriptively, without statistical comparison between groups or subgroups.Time to chemotherapy or death was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method.Statistical analysis was performed using SAS Enterprise Guide 8.2.
Results
Demographic and baseline clinical characteristics

A total of 29 Japanese patients in RELAY were aged ≥ 75 years (RAM+ERL, n = 12; PL+ERL, n = 17), corresponding to 13.7% of the Japanese ITT population (N = 211) (Table 1).A majority of patients in both treatment arms were female, with no history of smoking and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0. In the RAM+ERL arm, 50% of patients (6/12 patients) had an ex19del mutation and 50% (6/12) had an L858R mutation; in the PL+ERL arm, the proportions with these mutations were 29.4% (5/17) and 70.6% (12/17), respectively.
Overall response

Objective response rates and disease control rates in elderly patients were similar in both treatment arms (Table 2).The objective response rate (95% CI) was 83.3% (62.2%-100%) and 82.4% (64.2%-100%), and the disease control rate (95% CI) was 91.7% (76.0%-100%) and 100% (100%-100%), in the RAM+ERL and PL +ERL arms, respectively.Responses in the RAM+ERL arm were also similar in elderly patients with ex19del and L858R mutations.Among patients who responded (RAM+ERL, n = 10; PL+ERL, n = 14), the median (95% CI) duration of response was 17.5 (0.8-31.6) months in the RAM+ERL arm and 11.6 (5.6-17.7)months in the PL+ERL arm (unstratified HR [95% CI]: 0.81 [0.34-1.96]).
Exposure, dose intensity, and dose adjustments

Among elderly patients, the median duration of RAM or PL therapy was approximately 6 months, and the median relative dose intensity of RAM/PL was > 95% in both treatment arms (Table 3).The median (interquartile range) duration of ERL therapy was 15.4 (2.6-31.8)months in elderly patients treated Among the 12 elderly patients treated with RAM+ERL, eight (66.7%) had at least one dose adjustment of RAM and nine (75.0%) had at least one dose adjustment of ERL (Figure 1; Supplementary Table S2).Dose adjustments of RAM were mainly dose delays (six patients; 50.0%) related to blood bilirubin increased (two patients), dermatitis acneiform, herpes zoster, hyperkalemia, hypertension, malaise, neutrophil count decreased, occult blood, peripheral edema, paronychia, proteinuria, tracheitis, and upper respiratory tract infection (one patient each).A swimmer plot of dose adjustments in the RAM+ERL arm indicated that the dose of RAM was reduced from 10 mg/kg in two elderly patients; one patient had RAM reduced to 8 mg/kg and then to 6 mg/kg after an AE of proteinuria, and another patient had RAM reduced to 8 mg/kg after an AE of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) increased (Figure 1).Two patients (16.7%) had a RAM dose omission (one due to an AE of proteinuria and one due to the patient's decision).Dose adjustments of ERL were dose omissions (eight patients; 66.7%) or dose reductions (seven patients; 58.3%) related to dermatitis acneiform, ALT increased, paronychia, decreased appetite, rash, herpes zoster, and upper respiratory tract infection.The dose of ERL was reduced from 150 mg in seven patients after the AEs described above; of these, the final dose of ERL before discontinuation of study treatment was 100 mg in two patients and 50 mg in five patients.
Safety

All elderly patients in both treatment arms had at least one TEAE (Table 4).In both treatment arms, the most common TEAEs were dermatitis acneiform and diarrhea (Table 5).Although the incidence of specific TEAEs was generally similar in both treatment arms, proteinuria occurred exclusively in the RAM+ERL arm (six patients; any grade: 50%, grade ≥ 3: 0%).The rate of discontinuation of all study treatment due to an AE was similar in the RAM+ERL (four patients; 33.3%) and PL+ERL (six patients; 35.3%) arms (Table 4).AEs leading to discontinuation of all study treatment were ALT increased (two patients), paronychia, and cerebrovascular ischemia in the RAM+ERL arm, and acute cholangitis, gastric ulcer, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased, thromboembolic event, rash, and erythematous rash in the PL+ERL arm.

No TEAEs of ILD or pneumonitis were observed in elderly patients in the RAM+ERL arm, whereas one patient (5.9%) in the PL+ERL arm had three TEAEs of ILD -one event each at grade 1, grade 3, and grade 5 (fatal) -the last of which occurred more than 30 days after discontinuation of study treatment.

Grade ≥ 3 TEAEs were reported in 83.3% and 70.6% of patients treated with RAM+ERL and PL+ERL, respectively; all were considered related to study treatment (Table 4).The most common grade ≥ 3 TEAE in the RAM+ERL arm was ALT increased (four patients; 33.3%), which occurred in three patients (17.6%) in the PL+ERL arm (Table 5).

Serious AEs (SAEs) occurred in five (41.7%) patients in the RAM+ERL arm and six (35.3%) patients in the PL+ERL arm; three (25.0%)patients in the RAM+ERL arm and one (5.9%)patient in the PL+ERL arm discontinued all study treatment because of SAEs (Table 4).SAEs occurring in the RAM+ERL arm included ALT increased (two patients), pneumothorax, pleurisy, AST increased, neck pain, cerebral ischemia, and decreased appetite (one patient each).SAEs occurring in the PL+ERL arm included gastroesophageal reflux, cataract, acute cholangitis, infectious pleural effusion, retinal detachment, depressed level of consciousness, ILD, nausea, and duodenal ulcer (one patient each).There were no AEs leading to death while on study treatment or within 30 days of discontinuation of study treatment in either treatment arm.
Post-study treatment discontinuation therapies

The most common reasons for discontinuation of all study treatment were progressive disease (RAM+ERL: seven patients, 58.3%; PL+ERL: nine patients, 52.9%) and AEs (RAM+ERL: four patients, 33.3%: PL+ERL: six patients, 35.3%).All 12 elderly patients in the RAM+ERL arm received an EGFR-TKI as their first post-study treatment discontinuation therapy (Figure 2); of these, nine received ERL and three received gefitinib.Six patients received osimertinib and six patients received chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy as a second or later subsequent therapy.As of the final data cutoff, two patients were continuing treatment with a first-generation EGFR-TKI, one with ERL and one with gefitinib.
Time to chemotherapy or death
The median (95% CI) time to chemotherapy or death in elderly patients was 35.0 (8.7-48.7)months in the RAM+ERL arm and 20.7 (9.9-61.4)months in the PL+ERL arm.
Discussion

In this post hoc analysis of the RELAY trial, we examined the safety and efficacy of RAM+ERL in Japanese patients aged ≥ 75 years.This is the first analysis to evaluate the risks and benefits of an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitorbased combination therapy in elderly Japanese patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC.Elderly Japanese patients benefited from RAM+ERL to a similar extent as the Japanese ITT population.Median treatment duration of RAM and ERL was 6.0 and 15.4 months, respectively.RAM and/or ERL doses were adjusted in most elderly patients.Patients received various and multiple subsequent therapies, most commonly EGFR-TKIs including osimertinib, after the firstline study treatment.Moreover, no new safety concerns were identified in this age group.Taken together, these results suggest that physicians should not be deterred from considering RAM+ERL for elderly patients with EGFRmutated NSCLC solely because of patient age.Elderly patients may be at higher risk of experiencing AEs than younger patients, especially when considering toxicities related to cytotoxic chemotherapy [4].In this analysis of data from RELAY, the incidence of TEAEs among elderly Japanese patients was generally similar in both treatment arms, although low-grade proteinuria was only observed in the RAM+ERL arm.The incidence of grade ≥ 3 TEAEs was higher in the RAM+ERL arm (83.3%) than in the PL+ERL arm (70.6%); however, there were no AEs leading to death in either treatment arm, and the only ILD or pneumonitis event was in the PL+ERL arm.In addition, the most common types of TEAEs in the RAM+ERL arm were manageable and, unlike ILD, did not interfere with transition to second-line therapies.Moreover, discontinuation of all study treatment due to an AE occurred at a similar rate in both treatment arms.Overall, the safety profile of RAM+ERL in elderly Japanese patients was consistent with the Japanese ITT population [16,17].These results, consistent with findings from the REVEL trial, in which the combination of RAM and docetaxel was evaluated as second-line therapy for NSCLC [24], suggest that age alone should not deter the use of antiangiogenic agents.

In the present analysis, we confirmed that the objective response rates in elderly patients (83.3% and 82.4% in RAM +ERL and PL+ERL, respectively) were consistent with the RELAY global and Japanese ITT populations (approximately 76% and 75% in RAM+ERL and PL+ERL, respectively, in the primary analysis of both global and Japanese ITT populations) [15,16].

As reported previously [17], OS in RELAY elderly Japanese patients was generally consistent with OS observed in the global [14] and Japanese [17] ITT populations.The median (95% CI) OS in elderly Japanese patients treated with RAM +ERL was 44.2 (8.7-68.6)months [17], which may be considered favorable given that the real-world OSI-FACT-EP study of osimertinib as first-line therapy in elderly Japanese patients reported a median (95% CI) OS of 30.0 (25.8-37.7)months [25].Additionally, in age-based quintile analyses of the REVEL trial [24], the HRs for both PFS and OS favored RAM + docetaxel over docetaxel monotherapy in all age groups, including the oldest (≥ 70 years) [24].These results suggest that addition of RAM is effective in elderly patients.

In elderly Japanese patients in the RAM+ERL arm, the median (95% CI) duration of RAM treatment was 6.0 (1.4-24.9)months and median relative dose intensity was 95.1%; in elderly patients in the PL+ERL arm, median duration and median relative dose intensity of PL were 6.2 (2.4-15.4)months and 95.6%, respectively.Most elderly patients completed RAM treatment on the initial dose of 10 mg/kg, with dose reductions occurring in only two of the 12 patients, contributing to the high median relative dose intensity observed.The median duration of ERL therapy was 15.4 (2.6-31.8)months in elderly patients treated with RAM+ERL and 8.7 (5.4-19.3)months in those treated with PL+ERL, suggesting that addition of RAM did not negatively impact the treatment duration of ERL.Most patients required dose reductions of ERL, resulting in a lower median relative dose intensity for ERL in both treatment arms (RAM+ERL arm, 67.7%; PL+ERL arm, 67.0%).The median relative dose intensity of ERL in Japanese elderly patients was numerically lower than that observed in the Japanese ITT (77.8% and 79.3% in RAM+ERL and PL+ERL, respectively) [17] and the global ITT (92.6% and 95.8% in RAM+ERL and PL+ERL, respectively) [14] populations.The requirement for ERL dose reductions among many of the elderly patients is consistent with previous real-world studies of ERL and other EGFR-TKIs in older patients with NSCLC [26,27].Moreover, results from a previous pharmacokinetic analysis [28] suggest that the efficacy of ERL is not reduced by the need for dose reductions in response to AEs.Thus, appropriate dose reduction or interruption of ERL for the management of AEs allows for a longer duration of RAM+ERL treatment without compromising efficacy.

Treatment with RAM+ERL as first-line therapy allows for a range of subsequent therapy options, including osimertinib, other EGFR-TKIs, and chemotherapy, following study treatment discontinuation.Preservation of the effectiveness of these treatments allows for multiple subsequent lines of therapy and prolongation of survival.Importantly, in elderly patients, the delay in initiating cytotoxic chemotherapy also contributes to maintaining quality of life [4].In the current analysis, all 12 Japanese elderly patients treated with RAM +ERL received an EGFR-TKI as their first post-study treatment discontinuation therapy, with six patients (50%) later receiving osimertinib.The 100% transition rate to second-line therapy may be an advantage of RAM+ERL as the transition rate from first-line osimertinib was 39.6% (63/159) in the elderly group of the OSI-FACT-EP study [25].In RELAY, six elderly Japanese patients had chemotherapy as one of their post-study treatment discontinuation treatments, starting approximately 18, 27, 34, 36, 43, and 49 months after initiation of RAM+ERL treatment.The median time to chemotherapy or death in the elderly Japanese patients treated with RAM+ERL (35.0 [95% CI: 8.7-48.7]months) was similar to that observed in the RAM+ERL arms of the Japanese ITT (33.9[95% CI: 27.2-38.0]months) [17] and global ITT (33.1 [95% CI: 28.6-36.4]months) [14] populations.Thus, RAM+ERL allows elderly patients to have 35 months of chemotherapy-free survival.This is the first analysis of a phase III trial of combination therapy in elderly (aged ≥ 75 years) patients with previously untreated, metastatic, EGFR-mutated NCSLC as results for this age group from FLAURA2 or MARIPOSA have not been reported yet.Although sample size in this analysis was limited, this allowed detailed examination of treatment patterns in individual elderly Japanese patients over a long follow-up period.Importantly, as the choice of post-study treatment discontinuation therapy was at the investigator's discretion, these treatment patterns reflect the real-world clinical practice in Japan.However, it must be acknowledged that the analysis was post hoc and not designed to compare results between subgroups based on age or treatment.In addition, as age was not a stratification factor in RELAY, imbalances in patient characteristics (such as sex, smoking history, and EGFR mutation type) were found between treatment groups.
Conclusions
The results of this analysis of the RELAY trial suggest that RAM +ERL may be a suitable first-line treatment option for elderly Japanese patients with metastatic EGFR-mutated NSCLC.
